method: symmetric four-world authoring, post-hoc seeded key selection

items.setting: A left-luggage counter at a train station; a clerk behind the counter and a traveller with a suitcase.

worlds.keyAct: accept the setback and state a fallback plan
worlds.line: Sorry, our lockers are all full until about four this afternoon.
worlds.reply: I'll wheel it around town and try again after four then.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The clerk reports that storage is unavailable until a stated hour, so the traveller keeps the bag and names that hour as the moment to return. Answering with a bag count and a pick-up time responds to a question nobody asked, since nothing is being taken in. Thanking someone for redirecting to another floor fits no redirection, and promising to settle up later assumes a charge that was never quoted.

kills.1: "all full until" means nothing is being accepted for storage, so there is no count of pieces to declare or collection time to fix.
kills.2: "our lockers" places the storage service at this very counter, so the traveller has not been sent one floor down.
kills.3: "until about four" is about availability, not price, so there is no fee to settle up on collection.

worlds.line: How many pieces are you leaving, and until what time today?
worlds.reply: Two bags, and I'll collect them before six this evening.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The clerk asks for two pieces of information and the traveller gives both, a count and a collection time. Saying they will wheel the bag round town and return after four refuses a service that is being provided. Thanking someone for pointing downstairs fits nothing, since the drop-off is being processed here, and agreeing to settle up answers no stated price.

kills.0: "How many pieces" shows the bags are being taken in, so wandering off with the suitcase until four contradicts the transaction under way.
kills.2: "what time today" is the clerk here booking the items in, not sending the traveller to another floor.
kills.3: "How many pieces" asks for a count, and a promise to pay on collection supplies no count and no time.

worlds.line: That's the parcel desk — left luggage is one floor down, actually.
worlds.reply: One floor down — thanks, I'd have waited here all morning.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The traveller is at the wrong counter and the clerk relocates the service, so the reply repeats the new location and thanks them. A plan to return after four responds to a closing time that was never given. Naming two bags and a collection hour answers no question, and offering to settle up assumes a price this desk never quoted.

kills.0: "one floor down" means this counter has no storage lockers at all, so their being full cannot be the situation.
kills.1: "That's the parcel desk" is a redirection, not a request for the number of pieces or a collection time.
kills.3: "left luggage is" locates a service elsewhere; no fee has been mentioned to be paid later.

worlds.line: The charge is six euros a bag, payable when you pick it up.
worlds.reply: I'll settle up when I come back for them, no problem.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The clerk states the rate and when it falls due, and the traveller simply accepts that arrangement. Wheeling the bag around town until four would be a refusal of a service that is plainly being offered. Declaring two bags answers no question here, and thanking someone for sending them downstairs fits no redirection.

kills.0: "six euros a bag" prices storage that is clearly available, so full lockers are not the problem.
kills.1: "payable when you pick" states a payment term rather than asking how many pieces or until when.
kills.2: "The charge is" is this counter quoting its own rate, so the traveller has not been sent one floor down.

items.setting: A gate-change desk in an airport terminal; a passenger holding a boarding pass and the agent staffing the desk.

worlds.keyAct: give the new location and walking time
worlds.line: Is the Lisbon flight still leaving from B12, or has it moved?
worlds.reply: It's B27 now — roughly ten minutes' walk in that direction.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The passenger asks which gate the flight uses, so the agent names the new gate and how long it takes to reach. Radioing ahead to hold a door answers a timing crisis that has not been raised. A remark about a printer fits no request for a document, and amending a spelling fits no name that was mentioned.

kills.1: "still leaving from" asks which gate is in use, so nobody has said they cannot get to a gate in time.
kills.2: "or has it moved" seeks information, not a printed boarding pass.
kills.3: "the Lisbon flight" identifies a flight, not a passenger name, so there is nothing to correct.

worlds.line: I've just missed the shuttle, so I can't reach the new gate in time.
worlds.reply: I'll radio the gate and ask them to hold the door.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The passenger reports a transport failure that threatens boarding, so the agent contacts the gate to buy time. Being told the gate number and a walking time helps nobody who already knows the gate and cannot get there. A note about the reprint answers no request, and correcting a spelling addresses nothing that was said.

kills.0: "the new gate" shows the passenger already knows the gate has changed, so being given its number and a walk time is not an answer.
kills.2: "missed the shuttle" is a transport problem; no document was asked for.
kills.3: "can't reach the new" concerns arriving on time, not how a name is spelled.

worlds.keyAct: confirm the document will be produced
worlds.line: Could you print me a new boarding pass with the changed gate on it?
worlds.reply: The reprint will have the new gate printed on it.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The passenger asks for a fresh pass showing the change, and the agent confirms the reprint carries it. Simply naming a gate and a walking time leaves the request itself unanswered. Radioing ahead responds to a missed connection that was not mentioned, and amending a spelling addresses a name nobody raised.

kills.0: "Could you print" is an explicit request for a document, which naming a gate and a walking distance does not fulfil.
kills.1: "print me a new boarding pass" concerns paperwork, not a missed shuttle or a door held open.
kills.3: "with the changed gate" identifies the gate line as what must be right, not the traveller's name.

worlds.line: Actually my name is spelled with two Ns, not one, on there.
worlds.reply: I'll amend the spelling before you head through security.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The passenger flags an error in how their name appears, and the agent commits to correcting it before they move on. Being told a gate number and walking time ignores the error entirely. Radioing a gate to hold a door fits no missed connection, and a reprint described purely by its gate line does not address the misspelling.

kills.0: "two Ns" is about spelling, so this is not a question about which gate the flight uses.
kills.1: "spelled with two" raises a clerical error, not a missed shuttle or a boarding deadline.
kills.2: "my name is" identifies the name as the thing to fix, so a reprint praised for its gate line answers the wrong point.

items.setting: An intercity coach ticket window; a clerk at the glass and a traveller buying a fare.

worlds.line: There's a cheaper service at ten past, if you don't mind waiting.
worlds.reply: I'll wait for the later one, then — the fare matters more.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The clerk offers a lower fare in exchange for a wait, and the traveller takes that trade explicitly. Confirming a boarding bay responds to directions that were never given. Going off to find cash fits no payment problem, and stating that the trip is one way answers a question nobody asked.

kills.1: "at ten past" names a departure time as an option, not a boarding bay to walk to.
kills.2: "if you don't mind waiting" makes the choice about time and fare, not about how the ticket is paid for.
kills.3: "There's a cheaper" is an offer of an alternative service, not a question about the return leg.

worlds.keyAct: read back the directions and move off
worlds.line: The eleven o'clock coach boards from bay four, over by the kiosk.
worlds.reply: Bay four by the kiosk — I'll head over now.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The clerk locates the departure and the traveller repeats the bay and landmark before setting off. Choosing to wait for a later service fits no alternative that was offered. Fetching cash answers no problem with payment, and declaring a one-way trip answers no question.

kills.0: "boards from bay four" locates one departure; no second, cheaper service is put forward to wait for.
kills.2: "over by the kiosk" gives directions, and says nothing about how the ticket must be paid for.
kills.3: "The eleven o'clock" is the clerk supplying information, not asking whether the traveller returns today.

worlds.line: Sorry, this window only takes cash; the card machine is down.
worlds.reply: There's a cash point in the hall — back in a minute.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The clerk cannot take a card, so the traveller says where they will get cash and that they are coming straight back. Waiting for a cheaper service responds to an offer that was not made. Repeating a bay number fits no directions, and stating the trip is one way answers no question.

kills.0: "only takes cash" is about payment, not a choice between an earlier and a later coach.
kills.1: "the card machine" concerns the till at this window; no bay or boarding point has been named.
kills.3: "this window only" describes a restriction here, and nothing has been asked about the traveller's return.

worlds.keyAct: answer with the ticket type and reason
worlds.line: Are you travelling back today, or is this a one-way ticket?
worlds.reply: One way only — I'm staying with my sister all week.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The clerk needs to know whether to sell a return, and the traveller specifies one way and explains why. Waiting for a cheaper coach responds to an offer that was never made. Reading back a bay number fits no directions, and going for cash fits no payment obstacle.

kills.0: "travelling back today" is a question about the return leg, not an offer of a later, cheaper service.
kills.1: "a one-way ticket" concerns what to sell; no bay or kiosk has been mentioned to walk to.
kills.2: "Are you travelling" asks about the itinerary, and says nothing about how payment is taken.

items.setting: A hotel concierge desk in the evening; a guest at the desk and the concierge on duty.

worlds.keyAct: commit to arranging it and report back
worlds.line: Could you book us a table somewhere close for eight tonight?
worlds.reply: I'll try the bistro on the corner and confirm by seven.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The guest asks for a nearby dinner reservation at a set hour, so the concierge names where they will try and when they will report back. Extending the room responds to a change of dates that was never mentioned. Opening hours for a monument answer no dinner request, and a search of lost property fits nothing missing.

kills.1: "book us a table" is a dinner request, so there is no altered departure that would require lengthening the stay.
kills.2: "for eight tonight" fixes tonight's meal, not which day a monument admits visitors.
kills.3: "somewhere close for" concerns where to eat; nothing has been reported missing.

worlds.line: Our flight got moved, so we can stay a second night after all.
worlds.reply: I'll extend the booking and keep your key card working.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The guest's plans have changed in their favour, so the concierge handles the paperwork that follows and keeps their access alive. Trying a bistro and confirming by seven answers a dinner request that was not made. Monument opening days are beside the point, and lost property fits nothing reported gone.

kills.0: "stay a second night" reports a change of dates, not a request for a restaurant or a time.
kills.2: "Our flight got moved" concerns travel dates, not a monument's opening days.
kills.3: "a second night" is about the booking; nothing of the guest's has gone missing.

worlds.keyAct: answer and steer to the better day
worlds.line: Is the castle open on Mondays, or do we need Tuesday?
worlds.reply: Mondays it shuts at noon, so Tuesday suits you better.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The guest asks which day to visit, and the concierge gives the Monday restriction and recommends the alternative. Booking a bistro responds to a dinner request that was never made. Extending the booking fits no change of dates, and lost property fits nothing missing.

kills.0: "the castle open" makes this a sightseeing question, so no table or dining hour has been asked for.
kills.1: "on Mondays, or" is about planning a visit, not about lengthening the stay.
kills.3: "do we need Tuesday" concerns which day to go; nothing has been lost.

worlds.keyAct: open a search for the missing item
worlds.line: Someone's taken our umbrella from the stand by the lift.
worlds.reply: I'll check the lost property box and ask the porters.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The guest reports an item gone from a public stand, so the concierge starts the obvious search and involves staff who may have moved it. Trying a bistro answers no dinner request. Extending the booking fits no change of dates, and castle opening hours have nothing to do with it.

kills.0: "taken our umbrella" reports a loss, not a request for a table at a given hour.
kills.1: "from the stand" concerns something missing in the hotel, not a changed flight or an extra night.
kills.2: "by the lift" places the problem inside the building, not at a monument with opening days.

items.setting: The loading ramp of a small car-and-bike ferry; a deckhand directing traffic and a cyclist waiting to board.

worlds.keyAct: read back the instruction and comply
worlds.line: Wheel it up the ramp and strap it to the rail on the left.
worlds.reply: Straps on the left rail — I'll do that now.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The deckhand tells the cyclist where to put the bike and how to secure it, and the cyclist repeats the fixing point before doing it. Riding round to the stern answers a redirection that was not made. Accepting a later sailing fits no shortage of space, and a count of panniers answers no question.

kills.1: "up the ramp" sends the cyclist up this ramp, so no correction toward the stern is being made.
kills.2: "strap it to the rail" assigns the bike a place, so the deck is plainly not full.
kills.3: "on the left" is an instruction about securing the bike, not a question about luggage.

worlds.line: Not that ramp — bikes load at the stern, cars use this one.
worlds.reply: The stern, right. I'll ride round the back.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The cyclist has approached the vehicle ramp, so the deckhand redirects them and the cyclist confirms the new loading point. Talking about straps on a left-hand rail fits no instruction to secure anything here. Agreeing to a later sailing fits no full deck, and a count of panniers answers nothing.

kills.0: "bikes load at the stern" sends the cyclist elsewhere, so no rail here has been named to strap the bike to.
kills.2: "cars use this one" is about which ramp serves what, not about the bike deck being full.
kills.3: "Not that ramp" corrects a position; nothing has been asked about panniers.

worlds.line: The bike deck's full already; you'd be waiting for the four o'clock.
worlds.reply: I'll take the four o'clock — nothing else I can do.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The deckhand says this sailing is beyond capacity and names the next one, so the cyclist accepts it. Repeating straps and a left rail fits no instruction to secure a bike that cannot board. Riding round to the stern answers no redirection, and a count of panniers answers no question.

kills.0: "deck's full already" means there is no place aboard, so there is no rail to strap the bike to.
kills.1: "waiting for the four o'clock" makes the problem capacity, not which ramp to use.
kills.3: "The bike deck's full" concerns space aboard, not whether the bike carries luggage.

worlds.line: Are you carrying panniers, or is the bike going on empty?
worlds.reply: Two panniers, but I can take them off if needed.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The deckhand needs to know the bike's load, so the cyclist gives the number and offers to remove them. Confirming straps on a left rail responds to an instruction that was not given. Riding to the stern fits no redirection, and accepting a later sailing fits no report that the deck is full.

kills.0: "carrying panniers" asks about the load, not where to strap the bike.
kills.1: "going on empty" concerns luggage, so no redirection to the stern has been made.
kills.2: "Are you carrying" is a question about the bike's load, not news that the deck is full.

items.setting: The reception desk of a mountain hut in the evening; the warden behind the desk and a hiker just arrived.

worlds.keyAct: take up the offer and give a reason
worlds.line: We keep spare wool blankets behind the stove if you're cold.
worlds.reply: I'll grab one — the dorm windows don't seal well.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The warden offers extra bedding, and the hiker accepts and explains why the extra warmth is needed. Relief at avoiding the floor responds to news about a reserved bunk that was never given. Muddy boots fit no instruction about the rack, and agreeing on six fits no mealtime correction.

kills.1: "spare wool blankets" is an offer of bedding, and says nothing about companions having kept a bunk free.
kills.2: "behind the stove" locates blankets, not a boot rack or a rule about footwear.
kills.3: "if you're cold" concerns warmth, so no serving time has been stated to be corrected.

worlds.line: Your friends arrived an hour ago and saved you a bunk.
worlds.reply: That saves me a night on the floor, then.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The warden reports that a sleeping place has been held, and the hiker reacts to what that spares them. Fetching a blanket because of draughty windows responds to an offer of bedding that was not made. Knocking mud off boots fits no instruction, and confirming six fits no mealtime.

kills.0: "saved you a bunk" is news about a sleeping place, not an offer of blankets to collect.
kills.2: "Your friends arrived" reports who is here, not a rule about leaving boots anywhere.
kills.3: "an hour ago" fixes an arrival time, not the hour that a meal is served.

worlds.keyAct: comply and improve on the request
worlds.line: Please leave your boots on the rack before you go upstairs.
worlds.reply: They're pretty muddy — I'll knock them off outside first.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The warden asks for boots to be left downstairs, and the hiker agrees while proposing to clean them before doing so. Collecting a blanket responds to an offer that was never made. Relief about a bunk fits no news of one, and confirming six fits no stated mealtime.

kills.0: "on the rack" states a rule about footwear, not an offer of bedding from behind the stove.
kills.1: "leave your boots" concerns the hiker's own kit, not the arrival of friends or a saved bunk.
kills.3: "before you go upstairs" is about where boots go, not when supper is served.

worlds.line: Half board starts at six, not seven — the sign upstairs is old.
worlds.reply: Six, then. I'll come down straight after washing.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The warden corrects a mealtime the hiker would have taken from an outdated sign, and the hiker adopts the earlier hour. Fetching a blanket answers an offer that was not made. Relief about a bunk fits no such news, and muddy boots fit no request about the rack.

kills.0: "Half board starts" corrects a mealtime; no blankets have been offered to collect.
kills.1: "not seven" fixes an hour, and says nothing about friends arriving or a bunk being held.
kills.2: "the sign upstairs" concerns the posted time, not boots or where they must be left.

items.setting: A firewood kiosk at a campground; the attendant at the hatch and a camper buying wood.

worlds.line: We've just restocked, so there's dry birch again this evening.
worlds.reply: I'll take two bundles before it goes again.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The attendant reports that good wood is back in stock, so the camper buys immediately, before it sells out. Naming a pitch answers a delivery offer that was never made. A promise to put the fire out by a certain hour answers no rule that was stated, and returning a crate fits nothing handed over.

kills.1: "just restocked" is news about supply, so no delivery to a pitch has been offered that needs an address.
kills.2: "dry birch again" concerns what is for sale, not any curfew for putting fires out.
kills.3: "this evening" describes availability tonight; no crate has been given out to bring back.

worlds.keyAct: accept and give the delivery address
worlds.line: I can drop a load at your pitch on the quad bike.
worlds.reply: Pitch nineteen, by the washblock — that'd save me a trip.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The attendant offers to deliver, so the camper supplies the pitch and a landmark and welcomes the saving. Buying two bundles before stock runs out responds to a restocking announcement that was not made. A curfew promise answers no rule, and returning a crate fits nothing lent.

kills.0: "on the quad bike" makes this about getting the wood delivered, not about how much stock has come in.
kills.2: "at your pitch" concerns where to deliver, not when fires must be extinguished.
kills.3: "I can drop" is an offer to carry wood out, not a loan of any container to return.

worlds.line: Fires have to be out by eleven, ranger's orders.
worlds.reply: We'll douse it before then; we're early risers anyway.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The attendant states the site curfew, and the camper undertakes to comply and explains that it suits them. Buying two bundles before they go responds to no announcement about stock. Giving a pitch number answers no offer of delivery, and returning a crate fits nothing lent.

kills.0: "out by eleven" states a curfew, not an announcement that fresh wood has arrived.
kills.1: "ranger's orders" is a site rule, so no delivery has been offered that would need a pitch number.
kills.3: "Fires have to" concerns the fire itself; no crate has changed hands.

worlds.keyAct: agree and name when it will happen
worlds.line: Could you bring the crate back when you've emptied it?
worlds.reply: I'll return it on my way to the showers tomorrow.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The attendant asks for the container back, and the camper agrees and says when it will happen. Buying two bundles before stock goes responds to no restocking news. Giving a pitch and a landmark answers no delivery offer, and a curfew promise answers no rule that was stated.

kills.0: "bring the crate back" is about the container, not about how much wood is in stock.
kills.1: "when you've emptied it" concerns returning something, not delivering wood to a pitch.
kills.2: "the crate back" is a request about kit; nothing has been said about when fires must be out.

items.setting: A bike-share help point on a city street; a rider at the intercom and the staffer answering it.

worlds.keyAct: perform the action remotely and prompt a check
worlds.line: Can you unlock dock seven? The screen keeps rejecting my card.
worlds.reply: I've released it from here — try lifting the bike now.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The rider cannot release a bike and asks for help, so the staffer unlocks it remotely and asks them to test it. Closing a trip manually answers a billing record that was never mentioned. Instructions about tagging a broken bike fit nothing damaged, and a remark about route times answers no request.

kills.1: "unlock dock seven" asks for a bike to be let out now, so no finished trip is sitting open on the record.
kills.2: "rejecting my card" is a payment-screen fault, not a damaged bike being taken to a depot.
kills.3: "Can you unlock" is a request for action, not a remark about how long a journey took.

worlds.keyAct: close the record from the staff side
worlds.line: The app says I'm still riding, but I docked twenty minutes ago.
worlds.reply: I can see the dock time; I'll close the trip manually.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The rider reports that the record disagrees with what actually happened, so the staffer checks the logged dock time and ends the trip. Releasing a dock helps nobody whose bike is already returned. Tagging a broken bike fits nothing damaged, and a comment about route times answers nothing raised.

kills.0: "I docked twenty minutes ago" means the bike is already in a dock, so nothing needs unlocking.
kills.2: "The app says" makes this a record problem, not a faulty bike being wheeled to a depot.
kills.3: "twenty minutes ago" concerns a billing record, not how fast a route rides.

worlds.keyAct: decline the offer and give the procedure
worlds.line: I'll wheel this broken one back to the depot if that helps.
worlds.reply: Just tag it and leave it — our van collects tomorrow.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The rider offers to move a faulty bike, and the staffer waves the effort off and gives the standard procedure instead. Releasing a dock responds to no request to unlock anything. Closing a trip fits no open record, and a remark about journey times answers nothing.

kills.0: "this broken one" shows the rider already has a bike in hand, so no dock needs opening.
kills.1: "back to the depot" is about moving a faulty bike, not about a trip left open in the app.
kills.3: "if that helps" offers labour, and says nothing about how long a ride took.

worlds.line: The new bike lane means I made it here in ten minutes.
worlds.reply: It's cut most riders' times; the whole route reopened Monday.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The rider remarks on how quick the new lane made their journey, and the staffer generalises it and adds when the route reopened. Releasing a dock answers no request to unlock anything. Closing a trip fits no disputed record, and tagging a broken bike fits nothing faulty.

kills.0: "The new bike lane" makes this a remark about the route, not a request to unlock a dock or a card problem.
kills.1: "in ten minutes" reports a journey time, not a trip the app has left running.
kills.2: "made it here" describes arriving on a working bike, so nothing broken is being offered for return.

worlds.reply: Six-thirty suits us; we get off soon after that.

Asking to be woken twenty minutes early answers a question that was never put. A comment about spreading luggage fits no news about berths, and keeping hold of documents refuses an offer that was not made.

kills.2: "in your compartment" concerns where the meal arrives, not how many berths are occupied.
kills.3: "from six-thirty onwards" is about the morning meal, not an offer to hold anything overnight.

worlds.line: Do you want me to wake you before Vienna, or sleep through?

kills.0: "Two berths stayed empty" is news about occupancy, not a statement of when breakfast comes.

worlds.reply: I'd rather hold onto mine, thanks — I sleep lightly.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The attendant offers to take custody of documents overnight, and the passenger declines and gives a reason. Accepting a breakfast hour answers no service time that was stated. Choosing a wake-up margin answers no question, and a comment about spreading luggage fits no news about berths.

kills.0: "keep your passports" is an offer about documents, not an announcement about breakfast.
kills.1: "hand them back" concerns custody of papers, and proposes no waking arrangement to choose between.
kills.2: "at the border" is about the crossing, not about how many berths are occupied.

kills.2: "down into the boat" shows boarding is happening now, so no later departure time has been given to wait out.

worlds.line: Step over the rope, and keep your weight on the middle plank.

worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The boatman tells the passenger how to come aboard safely, and the passenger confirms the footing and says what they will do first.
